Well... when you add coverage and the number of people covered the costs do tend to go up. We're just beginning to see what the actual costs of Obamacare are so we shouldn't be surprised by cases like this.
An insurance company covering more people should not increase costs. That should make them less susceptible to statistical outliers like people who require cancer treatment and all.

It isn't just covering more people, the regulations have skyrocketed with obamacare. Surely you have heard that majority of a doctors staff is purely administrative to process insurance and Medicare claims. Do you think doctors want to pay to have three admins on their staff?

Incorrect, and I'll explain.

If you assume an insurer is expanding X group of people, and then expands to cover X + Y homogenous groups, then you're correct that covering more people will decrease per patient costs but minimalizing outliers.

However, the ACA did not do this. It forced insurers to cover non-homogenous groups at the same rate. Before the insurer could properly weight costs to risks, e.g. a 600lb hamplanet with diabetes would be extraordinarily expensive to insure if they could receive insurance at all, for obvious risk reasons (just like you don't lend $100,000 to a crackhead, because of the risk). The ACA changed this - now insurers can't reject applicants at all, and their hands are tied on per-person rate adjustments. So they charge everyone much higher rates to cover the overall increased risk of their insured.

TLDR: laws that force insurers to cover high risk people the same as low risk people result in dramatic price jumps for low risk people because freaking duh.

But it also requires everyone to get insurance, so a lot of healthy young people are also now getting insurance. Sure, some people don't get it and just take the penalty, but this, like many things, isn't as simple as "freaking duh".
It isn't simple that the ACA increases insurance costs for healthy insured? Uh...what?

Yes, it will increases insurance costs for the healthy young people who buy it on their own, relative to what it would have cost when those insurance companies could charge young healthy people less because they were young and healthy. But if insurance companies are able to charge less for young healthy people, they are able to charge waaaaaaay more for old or unhealthy people (or just turn them down outright). This is one of the things the ACA was trying to fix--it lets everyone pay the same amount, so that people who are older or who have pre-existing conditions can afford to get insurance without joining a big company that negotiates a group rate. It basically makes groups for people without them having to work for a big company. So yeah, it makes the rate for young healthy people go up, but it shouldn't make the average rate change much relative to what big group plans were previous to the ACA. I think a lot of people believe this to be a good thing, though--while you have to pay a little more in your youth & health, you'll be able to afford health care when you are old or have unexpected health problems. I know I sure don't want to be stuck with no affordable health care if my luck takes a turn for the worse.
